dispute.claim_text: I bought what was advertised as official skip-the-line entry tickets to the Alhambra. The booking page and confirmation described them as official monument entry. What I received was a voucher for a third-party guided walking tour that did not include entry to the monument. The seller presented itself as the official site. The purchase was not what was represented.

evidence.text: Screenshot of the purchase page: 'Official Alhambra Skip-the-Line Entry Ticket — direct monument admission.' Official-looking branding and crest.
Booking confirmation: 'Official Alhambra entry ticket, 2 adults, 2026-08-16.' Amount EUR 512.40.
Delivery email: 'Your Alhambra Area Guided Walking Tour voucher. Note: external tour; monument entry not included.'
Merchant reply to complaint: declines refund, cites 'strict no-refund policy' and EU consumer law; does not address the official-vs-third-party mismatch.
Screenshots of online reviews calling the company a scam that poses as official sites.

labels.notes: Hard case: sits on the 13.3/13.5 boundary. Classified 13.5 because the root wrong is misrepresentation of what was sold — the seller posed as the official vendor and represented 'official entry', then delivered a third-party tour — not a mere product-quality mismatch (which would be 13.3). Critical point 13.5-r1 strongly consumer-supported: listing + confirmation say 'official entry', delivery says 'tour, entry not included'. Merchant's no-refund policy and EU-law citation do not defeat 13.5 — the code supersedes merchant refund policy. ev_005 (reviews) is low-value color, deliberately not relied on for any point.
